tagline: Stone arches and forested buffers connect the city with parkland
intro: The New York stretch of the Palisades Interstate Parkway runs through Rockland and Orange counties, with stone arch bridges, wooded buffers and landscaped medians surviving from its original design. NYSDOT gives the state section a length of 26.58 miles and identifies historic, scenic and recreational qualities. It is both a State Scenic Byway and a National Scenic Byway; the Federal Highway Administration describes a drive designed to connect New York City with nature. The route serves commuters as well as park visitors.

Engineer William A. Welch developed the parkway proposal in 1933–34 to connect the New Jersey Palisades with parks farther north along the Hudson. John D. Rockefeller donated 700 acres in 1933, but the New Jersey Highway Commission’s opposition put the idea on hold. Rockefeller renewed the campaign with Robert Moses in the 1940s, and construction began in New York in 1947.

Driving south, start at the Bear Mountain Bridge traffic circle and pass through Bear Mountain State Park toward Harriman. The visitor center occupies a former median service area between exits 16 and 17. Beyond Harriman, continue past Stony Point and Mount Ivy to the Thruway interchange at West Nyack. The state section ends at the hamlet of Palisades on the New Jersey border.

moments.title: Bear Mountain Bridge
moments.text: Bear Mountain Bridge opened on November 27, 1924, with the world’s longest suspension span. That record lasted 19 months, until the Benjamin Franklin Bridge surpassed it. Earlier schemes had proposed a railway crossing; the company authorized in 1922 instead built for automobiles. Only the span between the towers hangs from cables; the approach spans are unsuspended. US 6, US 202 and the Appalachian Trail cross the Hudson here, where sidewalks flank the two vehicle lanes. It was the first automobile bridge over the Hudson south of Albany, and its construction methods influenced the later George Washington and Golden Gate bridges.

moments.title: Palisades Interstate Park Commission Visitor Center
moments.text: A former parkway service area now houses the Palisades Interstate Park Commission Visitor Center in the center median. It stands in Orange County between exits 16 and 17, north of the Lake Welch Parkway junction. The center offers information and a bookstore, with access from both directions.

moments.title: Harriman State Park
moments.text: Harriman’s lakes and roads owe part of their shape to public works during the Great Depression. Civilian Conservation Corps crews built roads, trails and camps, and worked on lakes including Welch, Silvermine and Pine Meadow. The park itself grew from Mary Harriman’s offer of 10,000 acres and $1 million in exchange for abandoning the state’s planned prison at Bear Mountain. The state agreed, and the deed and check were presented in 1910. Volunteers from the New York–New Jersey Trail Conference maintain more than 200 miles of trails. Lake Welch Parkway and Seven Lakes Drive connect with the Palisades Interstate Parkway within the park.

practical: Bear Mountain Bridge: Crossing the bridge eastbound requires an electronic toll. Payment uses E-ZPass or a mailed bill. (checked 2026-10-11)
Palisades Interstate Park Commission Visitor Center: Commercial vehicles are prohibited on the entire Palisades Interstate Parkway. (checked 2026-10-11)
